questions.q: Why does this lesson say a single "does it look right" pass is not real validation?
options: Because validation can only be performed by Salesforce Support
Because real validation checks several distinct levels (counts, completeness, referential integrity, spot-checks), each catching a different class of problem
Because validation rules must always remain active during a load
Because record counts are the only thing that ever needs checking
questions.explain: Each validation level catches something the others miss — a load can pass a record-count check while still having widespread field-level mapping errors, which is why multiple levels are needed.

questions.q: A load's record count exactly matches the expected count from the source extract. What does this lesson say that result does NOT guarantee?
options: That the load ran at all
That the source file was read successfully
That the job Id was generated correctly
That every field mapped and loaded correctly, since a value loaded into the wrong field can still produce a correct count
questions.explain: A correct record count is a fast, useful signal, but it says nothing about whether individual field values actually mapped and loaded correctly — that requires separate checks like spot-checking and referential integrity.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the responsible way to handle temporarily disabling validation rules during a load?
options: Disable them permanently, since legacy data will always need the relaxed rules going forward
Avoid ever disabling validation rules under any circumstances, even for one-time legacy exceptions
Treat it as a deliberate, documented, time-boxed decision, with an explicit, checked-off step to re-enable every rule immediately after the load
Disable them without documentation, since it only matters during the load itself
questions.explain: Disabling rules is a legitimate technique for handling messy legacy data, but it removes a safety net — using it responsibly means documenting exactly which rules, for how long, and explicitly re-enabling all of them afterward.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say relying on spot-checking alone is risky, even when the sample reviewed looks completely correct?
options: Because spot-checking only proves the specific sampled records are correct, not the whole load — a structurally consistent error in an unsampled category can pass unnoticed
Because spot-checking is not a real validation technique at all
Because spot-checking can only be performed after cutover, never before
Because spot-checking always requires disabling validation rules first
questions.explain: Spot-checking only proves the sampled records are correct. A widespread but consistent error affecting a mapping category outside the sample can pass completely unnoticed, which is why it's used alongside, not instead of, systematic checks.

questions.q: What does a referential integrity check specifically confirm?
options: That record counts match between source and target
That relationship fields are actually populated and point at real, correct records, rather than being empty or orphaned
That every required field is non-blank
That the Bulk API job finished within its 10-minute batch window
questions.explain: Referential integrity checks specifically verify that relationships (lookups/master-detail) are correctly populated, catching orphaned records that sequencing was supposed to prevent but that still slipped through.
